question: In 2021, an NFT of this meme's original 2010 photograph sold at auction for about $4 million, with some proceeds going to charities such as the Japanese Red Cross. Its canine subject, a female Shiba Inu, was rescued from a closing breeder around 2008 by a Japanese kindergarten teacher, narrowly avoiding being put down. That teacher's 2010 blog photo later inspired a joke cryptocurrency launched in December 2013 by Billy Markus and Jackson Palmer, which still uses the dog's face as its logo. Captions associated with this meme are written in broken English phrases like "such amaze" and "much wow," shown in multicolored Comic Sans font over photos of the dog. The dog behind it, often called the internet's most famous Shiba Inu, died in May 2024 at the age of eighteen after battling leukemia. For 10 points, name this internet meme depicting a smiling, side-eyeing dog.
answer: Doge [or Kabosu; do not accept or prompt on “Dogecoin”]

question: The music video for this song, posted to YouTube in August 2016 by a leopard-print-clad alter ego of Japanese comedian Kazuhito Kosaka, initially attracted little attention outside Japan. It went globally viral after Justin Bieber tweeted to his millions of followers that it was his favorite video on the internet, in late September 2016. At 45 seconds long, it became the shortest song ever to chart on the Billboard Hot 100, entering at number 77 and breaking a record set in 1964 by “Little Boxes”. Guinness World Records also recognized it for that same feat. Performed under the stage name Piko-Taro, for 10 points, name this novelty song whose title strings together a pen, a pineapple, and an apple.

This character was designed by then-recent art school graduate Emi Nagashima, credited under the pen name “Amy”, after a droopy egg yolk she was cooking reminded her of unmotivated young people. It debuted through an in-house design contest at its company, Sanrio, in 2013. Officially described by Sanrio as loving soy sauce and being left alone, it is often drawn wrapped in a strip of bacon like a blanket. Its Japanese name blends a word for “listless” with a shortened form of the word for “egg”. In December 2022, it got a Netflix stop-motion series called “An Eggcellent Adventure”. For 10 points, name this perpetually exhausted egg-yolk mascot made by the Japanese company Sanrio.

This meme's cat-shaped GIF was doodled on a 70-by-70-pixel canvas by Dallas-based illustrator Chris Torres, who based its face on his real-life Russian Blue cat. It is soundtracked by a sped-up Japanese song originally written for the Vocaloid voice Hatsune Miku. The viral video, though, uses a cover sung with a different voice synthesizer named Momone Momo. Torres posted the animation to his personal website in April 2011 under the handle “prguitarman”; the character's body resembles a frosted breakfast pastry. It ranked among 2011's most-viewed YouTube videos worldwide, sharing the top ten with clips like “Friday” and a “Talking Twin Babies” video. In February 2021, Torres auctioned a remastered version of the animation as an NFT for roughly $580,000. For 10 points, name this meme depicting a Pop-Tart-bodied cat flying through space, leaving a rainbow trail.

Since the 1970s, some of these Japanese coin-operated fixtures have offered dual-temperature service, dispensing both hot and cold canned drinks from the same unit, marked with red and blue tags. Certain models can be unlocked to hand out their contents for free during earthquakes and other disasters. Despite falling from a peak of about 5.6 million units around 2000, Japan's roughly 3.9 million of these still add up to the highest number per capita of any country. Besides drinks, some dispense curiosities like canned bread, hot corn potage soup, or bananas restocked daily by Dole. For 10 points, name these Japanese machines, found on nearly every street corner, that dispense drinks, snacks and other items for coins.

A 2012 revision to Japan's Animal Protection Law forced these businesses to close by 8 p.m., like other pet shops, until regulators granted an exception until 10 p.m. The concept was pioneered by Taipei's “Cat Flower Garden” in 1998, six years before Osaka's “Neko no Jikan” opened the first Japanese one, in 2004. Customers typically pay by the hour, historically around 1,000 yen, to relax with resident felines, appealing in cities like Tokyo, where strict housing rules make pet ownership difficult for many residents. America's first permanent one of these, Cat Town Cafe, opened in Oakland, California, in October 2014. For 10 points, name this type of Japanese cafe where patrons pay to spend time with resident cats.

This character and his giant robot were inducted into Marvel's mainline comic-book continuity through a 2014-15 crossover event that united heroes from many different parallel Earths. He gains his powers from the dying blood of an alien visitor, rather than a radioactive bug bite. To fight monsters that grow to giant size, he summons a 60-meter-tall robot named Leopardon, a format that Toei's Super Sentai franchise, the basis for the Power Rangers, would later borrow. Motorcycle racer Takuya Yamashiro played this hero across 41 episodes of a tokusatsu television series that aired in Japan from 1978 to 1979. For 10 points, name this Japanese television adaptation of a wall-crawling Marvel superhero, notorious among Western fans for how wildly different it is from the American comics.

In 2005, a specially thickened variant of this product, nicknamed “Space Ram”, was developed with Japan's space agency for zero gravity. It flew aboard the space shuttle Discovery, letting astronaut Soichi Noguchi become the first person to eat one in orbit. Its inventor, Momofuku Ando, had earlier invented the world's first instant noodles, “Chicken Ramen”, in 1958, after World War Two food shortages inspired him to make an easy, shelf-stable meal. Its innovation was a container that served as packaging, cooking vessel and eating bowl all at once, with noodles suspended partway up so boiling water could cook them evenly from below. It was launched by the company Nissin on September 18, 1971, and is now sold in more than 100 countries. For 10 points, name this global instant-noodle brand, eaten straight from its own container after adding hot water.

Coin-operated capsule machines like these were first imported to Japan from the United States in 1965, before Japanese toy company Bandai entered the market and trademarked its own version in 1977. Its name comes from Japanese onomatopoeia: one syllable for the sound of cranking the machine's handle, and another for the capsule dropping into the tray. Mobile games that let players spend virtual currency on randomized characters or items borrowed both this term and its randomized mechanic. That practice faced scrutiny from Japan's Consumer Affairs Agency, which outlawed “complete” versions that resembled gambling in 2012. Prizes inside are sealed in small clear plastic capsules, ranging from character figures and keychains to novelty items and stickers. For 10 points, name these Japanese capsule-toy dispensers, whose name is also used for a randomized loot-box mechanic in many mobile games.

In 2014, this character's biography sparked a stir after Sanrio told a cultural anthropologist that despite her ears and whiskers, she is “not a cat” but a fully personified character. Her canonical backstory gives her the name Kitty White, an English birthplace near London, and a pet cat of her own. Designer Yuko Yamaguchi has said she was drawn without a mouth so viewers could freely project their own emotions onto her blank face. She was first created in 1974 by illustrator Yuko Shimizu for the company Sanrio. For 10 points, name this bow-wearing icon whose face appears on everything from stationery to a Japan Airlines jet.

Whole fruit destined for this beverage is frozen with liquid nitrogen at minus 196 degrees Celsius before being pulverized and soaked in alcohol. Its manufacturing process extracts flavor from the entire fruit, including the peel, rather than relying exclusively on the juice inside. The Japanese version commonly contains nine percent alcohol, while its name also advertises the absence of sugar from the drink. Fruit juice, vodka and soda combine in this canned chu-hai brand, which is sold widely in Japanese convenience stores. For 10 points, name this potent Suntory canned cocktail whose two-word English name pairs an adjective for power with a number.

A former employee named Maimi Tanaka recorded the song “Miracle Shopping”, which became a recurring soundtrack inside this retail chain. One of its Akihabara buildings houses the theater where the idol group AKB48 performs, located on the eighth floor. Founded by Takao Yasuda, this business opened its first store under its familiar literary name in Fuchu in 1989. Its shops crowd merchandise from floor to ceiling and often stay open late, with a blue penguin serving as their mascot. For 10 points, name this Japanese discount retailer whose Spanish literary namesake is a would-be knight famous for attacking windmills.
answer: “Don Quijote” [or “Donki”; or “Don Don Donki”; or “Don Quixote”]

question: This character shares a cave with Usajii, an elderly rabbit whose habits provide a contrast to his unusual housemate. His favorite food is nikujaga, a Japanese stew combining meat and potatoes, and his spoken vocabulary consists of his own name. Tsuneo Goda created this character, who began appearing in short stop-motion station-identification films for a Japanese public broadcaster in 1998. A rectangular body covered in brown fur and a permanently open mouth lined with pointed teeth define this creature’s appearance. For 10 points, name this boxy monster mascot associated with NHK, whose name is often extended with a Japanese honorific.

An image of this mascot beside a bonfire became associated online with a caption jokingly attributing its actions to a demonic purpose. Its prefectural government allowed approved promotional uses without charging licensing fees, helping its image appear across a wide variety of merchandise. This character won the 2011 Yuru-chara Grand Prix, a competition that pits Japanese regional mascots against one another. Created in 2010, it helped promote tourism connected with the opening of the Kyushu high-speed railway through its home region. For 10 points, name this black bear mascot representing Kumamoto Prefecture, whose name begins with the Japanese word for bear.
answer: “Kumamon” [or “For the Glory of Satan”; or “For the Glory of Satan of course”; or “For the Glory of Satan Bear”; or “Satan Bear”]

question: This mascot cites Deep Purple’s Machine Head as its first album purchase and has also expressed enthusiasm for other heavy-metal performers. In its fictional biography, both parents are ordinary fruit trees, despite their offspring being able to speak and move around. A resident created this unofficial representative of Funabashi in Chiba Prefecture, and the character later headlined a performance at the Budokan. Unlike many silent costumed mascots, this energetic creature speaks in a shrill voice while jumping, shaking and sometimes headbanging. For 10 points, name this yellow pear fairy, an unofficial city mascot whose frantic performances made it a Japanese television celebrity.

A 2017 lip-sync recording by Dobbsyrules supplied a performance template later used to animate still portraits to this song. Deepfake clips using the First Order Motion Model helped turn this ballad into a widespread internet phenomenon during July 2020. Chess edits also use its mournful chorus at the moment a player makes a costly blunder on the board. Players can perform this karaoke number in entries of Sega’s Yakuza series, with Kazuma Kiryu providing a particularly recognizable rendition. For 10 points, name this melancholy karaoke ballad whose title means “like a fool”, also known online by its opening chorus phrase.
answer: “Baka Mitai” [or “Bakamitai”; or “Dame da ne”; or “Dame dane”]

question: Satoshi Sakurada drew inspiration for this restaurant chain from the cook-to-order approach he encountered at Original Tommy’s in Los Angeles. In 1987, this chain introduced a sandwich using compressed rice in place of bread, including a filling of ground chicken. Its expansion included Taiwan in 1989 and a Singapore outlet at Isetan Scotts in 1993, extending its reach beyond Japan. The three letters in its name stand for Mountain, Ocean and Sun, reflecting an explanation of the brand’s values. For 10 points, name this Japanese fast-food chain founded in 1972, especially associated with sandwiches that replace conventional bread buns with rice.

An almond-coated version of this snack followed the original in 1971, and a strawberry variety joined the range in 1977. Its name imitates the cracking sound made when someone bites through one of its slender, crisp pieces of biscuit. Glico began selling the original chocolate-coated version in 1966, establishing a product that would later be exported beyond Japan. Each piece leaves a small section at one end without coating, giving the eater somewhere to hold the snack. For 10 points, name these Japanese biscuit sticks, commonly sold in red boxes and mostly covered with a thin chocolate layer.

Miho Sasaki proposed the idea behind these machines at Atlus in 1994, although the suggestion initially failed to convince her superiors. A collaboration between Atlus and Sega brought the resulting machines to market in 1995, helping establish a new youth pastime. Their editing interfaces let customers add handwritten messages, decorative borders and drawings to pictures before receiving the finished output. Beauty effects associated with these machines can enlarge eyes and smooth skin, producing highly stylized portraits of friends posing together. For 10 points, give the Japanese name for these decorated photo-sticker booths, whose name abbreviates an English phrase about printing.

Aki Maita and Akihiro Yokoi received the 1997 Ig Nobel economics prize for their involvement in creating this unusual consumer product. Its name blends a Japanese word meaning egg with a term derived from the English word for a timepiece. Bandai released this product in Japan in 1996, followed by an international launch that brought it to many more children. Owners use three buttons to care for a creature whose hunger and happiness need attention as it grows on a small screen. For 10 points, name this egg-shaped electronic keychain toy in which neglecting a virtual pet can cause it to die.

Takeshi Okawara, an early manager for this chain in Japan, promoted party barrels as an alternative to an American turkey dinner. That seasonal idea expanded into a nationwide advertising campaign in 1974, helping turn a restaurant promotion into a recurring custom. In 1972, an outlet in Kobe helped this company develop a successful strategy targeting prosperous residential neighborhoods with expatriate customers. The chain’s Japanese business became particularly associated with December 24, when families purchase its food for a Western holiday celebration. For 10 points, name this American fast-food chain whose buckets have become a familiar feature of Christmas dinner in Japan.

Japanese postal-insurance employees learned about an American exercise program sponsored by Metropolitan Life, helping inspire this organized fitness practice. A Japanese version was introduced in 1928 in connection with Hirohito’s enthronement, linking public health with a national celebration. After an interruption following the war, a revised version returned to NHK in 1951 and became a familiar daily routine. Schools use these exercises in physical education, while some companies have employees perform them together as a group activity. For 10 points, name this Japanese practice of following broadcast exercise instructions and music, often performed together early in the morning.
answer: “Radio taiso” [or “Rajio taiso”; or “Radio taisou”; or “Rajio taisou”; or “Radio calisthenics”]

question: Much of this television program was filmed at the Midoriyama studios in Yokohama, with a character called General Tani leading contestants. Its original regular run began on TBS in 1986, and decades later a revival appeared through Amazon Prime Video. Contestants attempt increasingly difficult physical challenges, frequently losing their footing and ending up soaked or covered in mud along the way. The remaining challengers eventually take part in an assault against a comic count played by the comedian and filmmaker Kitano. For 10 points, name this Japanese obstacle-course game show whose title identifies the fortress belonging to its comedian host.

This comedy duo reached second place in the 2017 King of Conte competition only months after forming in May. Its members perform under the names Super Sansuke and Angora Soncho, with the former serving as the more conventional reacting partner. Their breakout routine uses a song by Ai Otsuka while one performer appears ready to demonstrate a jump-rope routine. At the musical climax, she unexpectedly abandons the expected skipping move for an odd dance, frustrating and eventually captivating her partner. For 10 points, name this Japanese comedy pair associated with a viral skipping-rope act, whose name combines a cat sound with a celestial object.

Enthusiasts developing these vehicles have repurposed components from sightseeing buses and American military equipment to create their elaborate exterior fittings. Examples existed among northeastern Japanese fishing-industry haulers before a series of Toei films helped spread the style during the 1970s. The 1975 film series Torakku Yaro popularized these vehicles by featuring drivers whose machines were far more ornate than ordinary freight transport. Their decorations often combine illuminated panels, colorful murals and extensive chrome or stainless-steel trim, with some vehicles remaining in commercial service. For 10 points, give the Japanese name for these extravagantly decorated trucks, often covered in bright lights and towering metal embellishments.
